title: the Atharva Veda's healing hymns
hook: the glass of water on a sickbed's nightstand gets its own hymns, and the Vedas part of the path closes there
tomorrow: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Atharva Veda's healing hymns turned to the plants: brown, white, red, dappled, dark, and called mothers. Which plant did you learn by name? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-five.

A glass of water on a nightstand. It's the first thing reached for in the morning and the last thing set down at night. Nobody calls it medicine. It's just there, sweating a ring onto the wood. The Atharva Veda doesn't overlook it. In its first book, among its healing hymns, are verses spoken to the waters. Today is also the last day on the Vedas themselves, so after the waters, a look back. Today: the waters that heal.
screen: `A GLASS OF WATER ON A NIGHTSTAND.` → `NOBODY CALLS IT MEDICINE.` → `THE VEDA DOES.`

segments.voice: One verse, in paraphrase: you waters are the ones who bring us joy; help us to strength, so that we may see great delight. Another goes further: within the waters is the deathless drink, within the waters is medicine. And another asks the divine waters to be kind to us, for our help and for our drinking. Put those together and water is three things at once. It's joy. It's medicine. And it's simply something to drink, blessed on its way to the mouth. The word for medicine there is bheshaja, the word inside the healer's all-healing hand from three days ago. In these hymns, remedy isn't locked away somewhere rare. It's in a hand, in a breath sent off, in the plants of an empty lot, in a cup of water. Now the look back. This stretch of the path began with what the Rig Veda is. Then the hymn of creation that ends asking who really knows. The Purusha Sukta. The Gayatri, in its setting. Hymns to Agni the fire, Indra, Ushas the dawn, and Varuna. The Sama Veda as song. And these healing hymns, which bring the Vedas down to a sickbed. Next, the path turns to Ayurveda, a classical Indian tradition of medicine, held here only as a lens for noticing, never as a diagnosis.
screen: `THE WATERS THAT BRING JOY.` · `IN THE WATERS, MEDICINE.` · `BHESHAJA: REMEDY, CLOSE AT HAND.` · `THE VEDAS, FROM CREATION TO A SICKBED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one slow sip. If there's water near you, pour a little. If not, hold the memory of a cool glass in your hand. Look at it first. Then take one sip, slowly, and follow it: cool on the lips, across the tongue, down the throat. Notice where it stops being something you feel. Then just sit, with the taste fading. If you pray, you can hold the waters in thanks. The bell holds the time.
The Atharva Veda's healing hymns. Hands, a cough sent flying, plants called mothers, and waters with medicine inside them. Today's word.
screen: `THE ATHARVA VEDA'S HEALING HYMNS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Atharva Veda's healing hymns. Today, when you drink water, let one sip be slow enough to notice all the way down. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Water is part of daily Hindu worship, offered to deities and to the sun and sprinkled for purification, and Vedic verses to the waters are recited in rituals of cleansing.

fork.setup: you're sick in bed in the world of these hymns. where does the Atharva Veda's first book say medicine is found?
options: only in rare herbs from far mountains
fork.reveal: within the waters is the deathless drink, within the waters is medicine. the remedy is in the glass by the bed.

original.note: Sanskrit: the waters, plural. The hymns speak to them as divine.

trapdoor: what you thought: medicine means pills and prescriptions.
what it means: in these hymns, bheshaja, remedy, is found close at hand: a kind touch, a breath, the plants, the waters.
what a scholar hears: apsv antar amritam apsu bheshajam, 'within the waters the deathless drink, in the waters medicine,' Atharva Veda 1.4.4.

notes: Editor: fixed a count error (the all-healing hand was day 1282, three days back, not two) and 'same family' to 'the word inside'; 'the classical' tradition of medicine to 'a classical'; cut 'anyone who has been sick knows that glass'.

Verse numbers AV (Shaunaka) 1.4.4, 1.5.1 and 1.6.1 given from memory (these verses also appear in the Rig Veda: 1.23.19, 10.9.1, 10.9.4; parallels left out of the script under the claims rule). Confirm.

Paraphrases: āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ ... mahe raṇāya cakṣase ('bring us joy ... that we may see great delight'); apsv antar amṛtam apsu bheṣajam; śaṃ no devīr abhiṣṭaya āpo bhavantu pītaye. Confirm renderings and the simplified transliteration.
'The same family as the healer's all-healing hand' links bheshaja to vishvabheshaja (day 1282); this is a compound, not an etymology, but confirm wording.
